{{Distinguish|Order of a polynomial (disambiguation){{!}}Order of a polynomial}}
The '''order polynomial''' is a [[polynomial]] studied in mathematics, in particular in [[algebraic graph theory]] and [[algebraic combinatorics]]. The order polynomial counts the number of [[order-preserving map]]s from a [[partially ordered set|poset]] to a [[total order|chain]] of length <math>n</math>. These order-preserving maps were first introduced by [[Richard P. Stanley]] while studying ordered structures and partitions as a Ph.D. student at [[Harvard University]] in 1971 under the guidance of [[Gian-Carlo Rota]].

== Definition ==

Let <math>P</math> be a [[Finite set|finite]] [[partially ordered set|poset]] with <math>p</math> elements denoted <math>x,y \in P</math>, and let <math>[n]=\{1<2<\ldots<n\}</math> be a [[total order|chain]] with <math>n</math> elements. A map <math> \phi: P \to [n] </math> is order-preserving if <math> x \leq y</math> implies <math>\phi(x) \leq \phi(y)</math>. The number of such maps grows polynomially with <math>n</math>, and the function that counts their number is the ''order polynomial'' <math>\Omega(n)=\Omega(P,n)</math>. 

Similarly, we can define an order polynomial that counts the number of [[strict]]ly order-preserving maps <math> \phi: P \to [n]</math>, meaning <math> x < y</math> implies <math>\phi(x) < \phi(y)</math>. The number of such maps is the ''strict order polynomial''  <math>\Omega^{\circ}\! (n)=\Omega^{\circ}\! (P,n)</math>.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Stanley|first1=Richard P.|title=Ordered structures and partitions|date=1972|publisher=American Mathematical Society|location=Providence, Rhode Island}}</ref>

Both <math>\Omega(n)</math> and <math>\Omega^\circ\!(n)</math> have degree <math>p</math>. The order-preserving maps generalize the [[Linear extension|linear extensions]] of <math>P</math>, the order-preserving bijections <math>\phi:P\stackrel{\sim}{\longrightarrow}[p]</math>. In fact, the leading coefficient of <math>\Omega(n)</math> and <math>\Omega^\circ\!(n)</math> is the number of linear extensions divided by <math>p!</math>.<ref name="Stanley1986"/>

== Examples == 

Letting <math> P </math> be a [[total order|chain]] of <math>p</math> elements, we have <blockquote><math>\Omega(n) = \binom{n+p-1}{p} = \left(\!\left({n\atop p}\right)\!\right)</math>  and   <math>\Omega^\circ(n) = \binom{n}{p}.</math> </blockquote>There is only one linear extension (the [[Identity function|identity mapping]]), and both polynomials have leading term <math>\tfrac 1{p!}n^p</math>.

Letting <math> P </math> be an [[antichain]] of <math>p</math> incomparable elements, we have <math>\Omega(n) =\Omega^\circ(n) = n^p </math>. Since any bijection <math>\phi:P\stackrel{\sim}{\longrightarrow}[p]</math> is (strictly) order-preserving, there are <math>p!</math> linear extensions, and both polynomials reduce to the leading term <math>\tfrac {p!}{p!}n^p = n^p</math>.

==Reciprocity theorem ==

There is a relation between strictly order-preserving maps and order-preserving maps:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stanley |first1=Richard P. |title=A chromatic-like polynomial for ordered sets |date=1970 |journal=Proc. Second Chapel Hill Conference on Combinatorial Mathematics and Its Appl. |pages=421&ndash;427}}</ref>
:<math>\Omega^\circ(n) = (-1)^{|P|}\Omega(-n).</math>

In the case that <math>P</math> is a chain, this recovers the [[Binomial coefficient#Generalization to negative integers n|negative binomial identity]]. There are similar results for the [[chromatic polynomial]] and [[Ehrhart polynomial]] (see below), all special cases of Stanley's general [[Stanley's reciprocity theorem|Reciprocity Theorem]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Enumerative combinatorics. Volume 1|last1=Stanley | first1=Richard P.|date=2012|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=9781139206549|edition=2nd|location=New York|chapter=4.5.14 Reciprocity theorem for linear homogeneous diophantine equations|oclc=777400915}}</ref>

== Connections with other counting polynomials ==

===Chromatic polynomial ===

The [[chromatic polynomial]] <math>P(G,n)</math>counts the number of proper [[Graph coloring|colorings]] of a finite [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] <math>G</math> with <math>n</math> available colors. For an [[acyclic orientation]] <math>\sigma</math> of the edges of <math>G</math>, there is a natural "downstream" partial order on the vertices <math>V(G) </math> implied by the basic relations <math> u > v </math> whenever <math>  u \rightarrow v </math> is a directed edge of <math>\sigma</math>. (Thus, the [[Hasse diagram]] of the poset is a subgraph of the oriented graph <math>\sigma</math>.) We say <math>\phi: V(G) \rightarrow [n] </math> is compatible with <math>\sigma</math> if <math>\phi</math> is order-preserving. Then we have 

:<math> P(G,n) \ =\ \sum_{\sigma} \Omega^\circ\!(\sigma,n),</math>

where <math>\sigma</math> runs over all acyclic orientations of ''G,'' considered as poset structures.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Stanley|first1=Richard P.|title=Acyclic orientations of graphs|journal=[[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]]|date=1973|volume=5|issue=2|pages=171–178|doi=10.1016/0012-365X(73)90108-8|doi-access=}}</ref>

=== Order polytope and Ehrhart polynomial ===
{{main|Order polytope}}
The [[order polytope]] associates a [[polytope]] with a partial order. For a poset <math>P</math> with <math>p</math> elements, the order polytope <math>O(P)</math> is the set of order-preserving maps <math>f:P\to [0,1]</math>, where <math>[0,1] = \{ t\in\mathbb{R}\mid 0\leq t\leq 1\}</math> is the ordered [[unit interval]], a continuous chain poset.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Alexander |last1=Karzanov |first2=Leonid |last2=Khachiyan |title=On the conductance of Order Markov Chains |journal=[[Order (journal)|Order]] |volume=8 |pages=7&ndash;15 |year=1991 |doi=10.1007/BF00385809|doi-access=|s2cid=120532896 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first1=Graham |last1=Brightwell |first2=Peter |last2=Winkler |title=Counting linear extensions |journal=[[Order (journal)|Order]] |volume=8 |pages=225&ndash;242 |year=1991 |issue=3 |doi=10.1007/BF00383444|doi-access=|s2cid=119697949 }}</ref> More geometrically, we may list the elements <math>P=\{x_1,\ldots,x_p\}</math>, and identify any mapping <math>f:P\to\mathbb R</math> with the point <math>(f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_p))\in \mathbb{R}^{p}</math>; then the order polytope is the set of points <math>(t_1,\ldots,t_p)\in [0,1]^p</math> with  <math>t_i \leq t_j</math> if <math>x_i \leq x_j</math>.<ref name="Stanley1986">{{Cite journal|last=Stanley|first=Richard P.|date=1986|title=Two poset polytopes|journal=[[Discrete & Computational Geometry]]|volume=1|pages=9–23|doi=10.1007/BF02187680|doi-access=free}}</ref> 

The [[Ehrhart polynomial]] counts the number of [[integer lattice]] points inside the dilations of a [[polytope]]. Specifically, consider the lattice <math>L=\mathbb{Z}^n</math> and a <math>d</math>-dimensional polytope <math>K\subset\mathbb{R}^d</math> with vertices in <math>L</math>; then we define

:<math>L(K,n) = \#(nK \cap L),</math>

the number of lattice points in <math>nK</math>, the dilation of <math>K</math> by a positive integer scalar <math>n</math>. [[Eugène Ehrhart|Ehrhart]] showed that this is a [[rational function|rational polynomial]] of degree <math>d</math> in the variable <math>n</math>, provided <math>K</math> has vertices in the lattice.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Computing the continuous discretely|title-link= Computing the Continuous Discretely |last1=Beck|first1=Matthias|last2=Robins|first2=Sinai|publisher=Springer|year=2015|isbn=978-1-4939-2968-9|location=New York|pages=64–72}}</ref>

In fact, the Ehrhart polynomial of an order polytope is equal to the order polynomial of the original poset (with a shifted argument):<ref name="Stanley1986" /><ref>{{cite journal|last=Linial|first=Nathan|year=1984|title=The information-theoretic bound is good for merging|journal=SIAM J. Comput.|volume=13|issue=4|pages=795&ndash;801|doi=10.1137/0213049}}<br />{{cite journal
 | last1 = Kahn | first1 = Jeff
 | last2 = Kim | first2 = Jeong Han
 | doi = 10.1006/jcss.1995.1077
 | issue = 3
 | journal = Journal of Computer and System Sciences
 | pages = 390–399
 | title = Entropy and sorting.
 | volume = 51
 | year = 1995| doi-access = free
 }}</ref><blockquote><math>L(O(P),n)\ =\ \Omega(P,n{+}1).</math></blockquote>This is an immediate consequence of the definitions, considering the embedding of the <math>(n{+}1)</math>-chain poset <math>[n{+}1]=\{0<1<\cdots<n\}\subset \mathbb{R} </math>.
